title: Underrated CEO Skill: Knowing an Expert When You See One
author: Managing the Future
summary: This essay argues that the deep functional expertise which propels executives to the CEO role is often precisely what undermines them once they arrive, because the job requires breadth, delegation, and judgment exercised through other people rather than personal mastery of any one domain. The author's central example is the sales-leader-turned-CEO who keeps second-guessing the sales team because that is where his comfort and credibility lie, throwing the rest of the organization out of balance. Because CEOs must constantly evaluate competence in domains where they have little personal expertise, the piece offers five concrete diagnostic signals for spotting a real expert: they can describe exactly what they would do, they can explain it simply rather than in jargon, they can make working predictions, they know precisely where their knowledge ends, and they carry the earned respect of other credible people. The piece closes by acknowledging Steve Jobs and Elon Musk as rare exceptions who personally drove deep technical work, while insisting most CEOs who try to imitate that pattern create more problems than they solve; the real leverage of the role is curating and orchestrating expertise, not supplying it.
points: The central diagnostic claim: a CEO's own prior functional expertise is a liability risk, not an asset, because it pulls disproportionate attention toward the one function the CEO understands best, unbalancing the rest of the organization.

The five-signal method for spotting real expertise (detailed action plans, simplicity of explanation, predictive accuracy, known limits, and earned peer respect) gives leaders a repeatable evaluation tool for domains outside their own competence.
The essay reframes the CEO's 'real work' as curating and balancing expertise across the business rather than personally directing any one function, even one they are skilled in.

Jobs and Musk are explicitly named as exceptions that prove the rule: their personal technical mastery worked because it was paired with orchestration skill, not as a template for typical CEOs to imitate.
The PR-hire anecdote operationalizes the 'ask what they'd go do' technique as a portable interview method for evaluating expertise in any unfamiliar field.
quotes: As a CEO, you need breadth over depth, delegation over mastery, judgment exercised through other people rather than applied directly to the work.
